summary: Presents application-specific routing requirements for urban low-power and lossy networks, where sensing and actuating nodes are placed outdoors in cities to improve living conditions and monitor things like environmental rules. It informs what routing protocols must support.

plainLanguage.summary: Urban low-power and lossy networks connect sensors, actuators, and routers deployed around cities. RFC 5548 describes the traffic and operating conditions and lists what IPv6 routing protocols for these networks should support.

subtitle: Routing requirements for outdoor urban sensor and actuator networks with constrained devices and unreliable links.

tldr.problem: Urban sensor and actuator networks may contain many low-power devices that communicate over short-range, variable wireless links.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes network roles, traffic patterns, and requirements for scalable, autonomous IPv6 routing that can account for node capabilities and changing conditions.
tldr.outcome: This Informational document sets requirements for routing protocols in urban LLNs. It does not specify a routing protocol.

today: RFC 5548 is Informational and was published in May 2009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Devices and Conditions in an Urban LLN
sections.content:
An urban low-power and lossy network contains sensors, actuators, and routers. Sensors report measurements such as utility use, weather, or pollution. Actuators control devices such as street or traffic lights. Some routers, called Low-Power and Lossy Network Border Routers (LBRs), connect the network to wider infrastructure.

The RFC considers deployments from 10^2 to 10^7 sensing nodes, placed in batches and connected over variable wireless links. Nodes may have limited memory and energy, and distances between devices can range from several hundred meters to one kilometer. Not every field node can reach an LBR directly.
sections.plainLanguage: Urban LLNs connect many sensors and actuators through wireless routers. Devices may be far apart, energy-constrained, and unable to reach an Internet gateway in one hop.

sections.title: Traffic Patterns and Reporting
sections.content:
The RFC describes regular reports, queried measurements, and alerts. Regular reports may occur once an hour or once a day. Queries may need results within seconds or minutes, while alert deliveries within seconds should be sufficient in most cases.

Traffic is directional: sensor readings usually travel toward LBRs, while queries and control instructions travel toward sensors or actuators. A network may also need to carry bursts, such as alerts during a city-wide power outage, when nodes have limited temporary power and must forward other devices' messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Most sensor reports are periodic, while queries and alerts have different timing needs. Routing should account for traffic direction and bursts that affect many devices.

sections.title: Routing Protocol Requirements
sections.content:
The routing protocol must support large deployments organized into regions of about 10^2 to 10^4 sensing nodes, and must scale without performance falling below configurable thresholds. It must support parameter-constrained routing using node capabilities such as memory, CPU, or remaining battery energy.

The protocol must provide zero-configuration at startup, self-organization after topology changes, and unicast, multicast, and anycast. It must accommodate bursts by computing multiple paths to a destination. Local changes should not force the whole network to reorganize, and route convergence should be much faster than the smallest reporting interval.
sections.plainLanguage: Routing must scale to many devices, use node capabilities in route choices, and adapt to local changes. It must also support the traffic patterns and address-delivery methods the network needs.

sections.title: Authentication and Resource Protection
sections.content:
The RFC says routing security should be light enough to run on constrained nodes. A network must authenticate and authorize nodes before they participate in routing decisions, and the routing protocol must support message integrity.

The protocol should defend against denial of service, including forwarding loops and excessive control traffic. A single physically compromised node should not be able to deny service to the entire network. An urban LLN should not connect to an external network that has not established trust.
sections.plainLanguage: Only authenticated and authorized devices should influence routing. Security measures should limit the damage that one compromised node can cause.
